records.text: Weight reuse is the defining advantage of convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
In CNNs, the same filters are applied across the entire input and over all intermediate feature tensors.
Weight reuse dramatically reduces the number of parameters.
Weight reuse enables massive parallelism.
Before deep learning, convolutions were used as handcrafted filters in classical computer vision.
In classical computer vision, small matrices were slid over an image to perform operations such as sharpening, blurring, embossing, or edge detection.
Gabor filters compute discrete directional derivatives.
One Gabor filter fires on large vertical differences between adjacent pixels.
Another Gabor filter fires on horizontal changes.
Applying max pooling as an image filter would clamp to maximum brightness, producing unnatural results.
Average pooling appears smoother but is not meant to be a pixel-level transformation.
In ResNet-18, the first layer's convolutional filters can be inspected.
Some first-layer filters in ResNet-18 detect diagonal or vertical lines.
Some first-layer filters in ResNet-18 respond to colors or colour gradients.
In ResNet-18, when an input image is passed through, one filter might fire where green appears.
In ResNet-18, another filter might fire for horizontal edges.
Deeper in the network, direct pixel-to-feature correspondence disappears.
Each unit in a CNN has a receptive field.
Tracing exactly which pixels contribute to a unit's activation requires additional mathematics.
One can observe what upper-layer features respond to.
In ResNet-18, the second layer activates on high-frequency content (stripes, edges) across the whole image.
Deeper layers in ResNet-18 respond to more semantic structures: a filter might detect eyes and ear tips.
Even deeper filters in ResNet-18 fire on entire heads.
Visualizations of deeper features become progressively blurrier and less geometric.
The features can be mapped back to the original image to approximate what triggers them.
At a late layer, features can be strongly class-selective.
A cat-selective feature correlates strongly with the "cat" class on ImageNet.
If a composite image half-cat, half-dog is presented, the cat-selective feature fires on the cat half and a dog-selective feature fires on the dog half.
This demonstrates genuine selectivity.
GradCAM is a more detailed explanation method.
Given a classification network, running GradCAM on a specific class output reveals which pixels contributed most to that output value.
For example, the "Egyptian cat" logit in a network responds because of certain image regions, while the "Blenheim Spaniel" logit focuses on other regions.
GradCAM is not an attention mechanism.
GradCAM provides a post-hoc explanation of the network's decision.
AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton, 2012) was the architecture that kick-started modern deep learning for computer vision.
AlexNet dominated the ImageNet Large-Scale Visual Recognition Competition by an extraordinary margin.
In the ImageNet Large-Scale Visual Recognition Competition, competing methods had error rates around 22–23%.
AlexNet achieved an error rate of approximately 13% in that competition.
The following year, the entire leaderboard of the competition switched to convolutional networks.
Classical computer vision was abandoned for image classification.
Model parallelism was used for the first time at an industrial scale in AlexNet.
In AlexNet, the network was split into two parallel streams, each running on a separate GPU.
Data parallelism splits a mini-batch across GPUs, processes them in parallel, and then aggregates the gradients for a single update.
In data parallelism, the network implementation does not change.
Model parallelism is necessary when the model does not fit on a single GPU.
AlexNet was hand-engineered by Alex Krizhevsky to explicitly assign layers to different GPUs while minimising cross-GPU communication.
Cross-GPU communication is slower than on-chip communication.
In modern frameworks such as PyTorch, specific weight matrices can be assigned to specific GPUs and communication is handled automatically.
VGG (Oxford Visual Geometry Group) represents large convolutions as compositions of smaller ones, typically stacks of $3 \times 3$ convolutions.
Using a stack of $3 \times 3$ filters reduces the number of weights compared to one large filter.
Using a stack of $3 \times 3$ filters makes the network deeper.
Using a stack of $3 \times 3$ filters acts as additional structural regularisation because the network processes different parts of the input in the same way.
VGG was used in the ILSVRC-2014 competition.
NVIDIA later optimised GPUs especially for $3 \times 3$ convolutions.
The idea of treating a large convolution as a "convolution inside a convolution" proved very effective.
The Inception architecture and its realisation in GoogLeNet employ the "network in network" concept to reduce the number of weights even further.
Instead of using a single linear convolution over a tile, Inception units implement a more complex mini-network that is still applied identically across all spatial positions.
Another idea in Inception is to insert additional classifiers (and corresponding auxiliary loss terms) at intermediate layers of the network.
Inception units frequently feature multiple parallel processing branches.
In Inception v2 (Szegedy et al., 2015), $n \times n$ convolutions are replaced by $n \times 1$ followed by $1 \times n$ convolutions.
In Inception v2, filter banks become wider rather than deeper.
The same paper that introduced Inception v2 also introduced Inception v3.
Inception v3 adds RMSProp optimisation.
Inception v3 adds factorised $7 \times 7$ convolutions.
Inception v3 adds batch normalisation in the auxiliary classifiers.
Inception v3 adds label smoothing.
A regular classifier trains the softmax with a hard target $q(k) = [k = y]$ (a one-hot vector).
The hard target encourages the logits to grow without bound, leading to overconfident predictions and overfitting.
Label smoothing replaces the hard target with a soft target: $q'(k) = (1 - \epsilon)[k = y] + \epsilon u(k)$.
In the soft target, $u(k)$ is a prior distribution, often the uniform distribution $u(k) = \frac{1}{K}$.
Label smoothing prevents the network from becoming too certain and improves generalisation.
Residual learning addresses the vanishing gradient problem by training differences rather than the full mapping.
A residual unit computes $y^{(k)} = F(x^{(k)}) + x^{(k)}$.
In the residual unit, $x^{(k)}$ is the input to layer $k$.
In the residual unit, $F$ is the function learned by the layer.
In the residual unit, $y^{(k)}$ becomes $x^{(k+1)}$.
The gradient can flow directly through the identity path in a residual unit: $\frac{\partial y^{(k)}}{\partial x^{(k)}} = 1 + \frac{\partial F(x^{(k)})}{\partial x^{(k)}}$.
Because of the identity path, gradients do not vanish when $F$ saturates.
When a layer's output $F(x)$ saturates and its derivatives approach zero, without a skip connection all layers below would stop receiving gradients.
The identity shortcut in residual units guarantees a path for gradient flow, enabling extremely deep networks.
Kaiming He introduced ResNets.
Kaiming He called the introduction of ResNets the "revolution of depth".
AlexNet had 8 trainable layers.
VGG had 19 trainable layers.
GoogLeNet had 22 trainable layers.
ResNet immediately scaled to 150 layers.
After ResNet, networks of 200, 500, or even 1000 layers became trainable.
Practical ResNets typically go up to about 200 layers.
Highway networks (Schmidhuber) are a related approach to residual learning.
In highway networks, the output is a gated combination: $y^{(k)} = C(x^{(k)}) x^{(k)} + T(x^{(k)}) F(x^{(k)})$.
In highway networks, $C$ is a carry gate and $T$ is a transform gate.
In highway networks, usually $C = 1 - T$.
In practice, residual connections work best when they are as "straight" as possible.
Beyond the weight reduction achieved by VGG-style small filters, an even more aggressive parameter saving is possible via bottleneck layers.
A standard convolutional layer operates on a cut-out window of depth $D$, width $W$, height $H$, producing an output of depth $D'$.
The weight tensor size of a standard convolutional layer is $D \times W \times H \times D'$.
With small filters ($W = H = 3$) and moderate depths ($D = D' = 256$), a standard convolutional layer has approximately $256 \times 3 \times 3 \times 256 \approx 590\text{k}$ parameters.
A bottleneck layer first compresses the input channel depth with a $1 \times 1$ convolution to a much smaller dimension $D''$.
Then the bottleneck applies the spatial convolution.
Finally the bottleneck expands back to $D'$ with another $1 \times 1$ convolution.

If $D=256$, $D''=32$, $D'=256$, the parameter count of a bottleneck becomes $D \cdot D'' + D'' \cdot W \cdot H \cdot D'' + D'' \cdot D' = 256 \cdot 32 + 32 \cdot 32 \cdot 9 + 32 \cdot 256 \approx 25.6\text{k}$.
This parameter count is a 25-fold reduction compared to the full convolution without bottleneck.
Compressing a 256-dimensional feature vector down to 32 numbers and then decompressing back to 256 cannot restore lost information.
A single bottleneck branch would be senseless because one could simply let the previous layer produce 32 features instead and save even more weights.
The bottleneck idea becomes powerful when multiple parallel branches are used.

By creating several copies of the bottleneck block, each with its own independently learned weights, and concatenating their outputs, the network learns multiple low-dimensional projections of the same high-dimensional space.
The multiple low-dimensional projections learned by the parallel bottleneck branches capture different aspects of the data.

With $D=256$, $D''=32$, and 8 branches, the total parameter cost of the multiple bottlenecks is about $8 \times 25.6\text{k} \approx 205\text{k}$, compared to the original $590\text{k}$ – a 3–4 fold saving.
Geometrically, taking many learned random projections of a high-dimensional object is often beneficial.
In the bottleneck approach, the projections are trained to be useful.
The approach of using multiple parallel bottleneck branches is called split-transform-merge: split the input, transform each part, then merge the results.
Split-transform-merge is a standard pattern in convolutional architectures.
ResNeXt (Xie et al., 2016) replaces ResNet units with split-transform-merge units reminiscent of Inception.
In ResNeXt, the input channels are divided into groups, and every group receives its own convolutions.
This grouping is akin to group convolutions, already used in AlexNet for parallelisation.
Group convolutions in ResNeXt yield a kind of specialisation in the resulting feature maps.
Another paper (Szegedy et al., 2016) introduced Inception v4 and Inception-ResNet.
The Inception family long served as excellent backbones for many computer vision tasks.

When labelled data is scarce, the standard practice is to take a model pretrained on ImageNet for classification, cut off its classification head, and use the rest as a feature extractor, possibly with light fine-tuning.
Inception v4 standardises everything and simplifies the units.
In Inception v4, a "stem" module is defined first, followed by three basic blocks (A, B, C) and special reduction blocks to reduce spatial dimensions.

In Inception v4, instead of a fixed pooling operation, the reduction blocks are learnable compositions of layers with strided convolutions, often containing pooling internally and following the split-transform-merge pattern.
Inception-ResNet adds residual connections to Inception blocks.
In Inception-ResNet, there is no pooling, but reduction blocks are still employed, making the architecture even simpler.
Inception-ResNet v2 is a refined version that performs extremely well in practice.
Inception-ResNet v2 was one of the most widely used backbones around 2016.
When deploying networks, two resources must be balanced: memory (number of weights) and latency (number of sequential layers).
GPU parallelism means that the number of layers often dictates latency more than the raw parameter count.
Intermediate representation sizes also matter for deployment.
Real-time applications, such as surveillance tracking, require at least 30-60 frames per second.
The need for real-time performance drives the development of extremely efficient architectures.
SqueezeNet (Iandola et al., 2017) aims to drastically reduce the number of parameters.
SqueezeNet replaces $3 \times 3$ filters with $1 \times 1$ filters.
SqueezeNet reduces the number of input channels for the remaining $3 \times 3$ convolutions.
SqueezeNet delays downsampling as late as possible to keep activation maps large.
The core building block of SqueezeNet is the fire module.
The fire module is composed of a squeeze layer (only $1 \times 1$ convolutions) followed by an expand layer (a mix of $1 \times 1$ and $3 \times 3$ convolutions).
SqueezeNet yields about 50× fewer parameters than AlexNet, at the cost of some accuracy.
MobileNet (Howard et al., 2017) designs networks specifically for mobile devices.
MobileNet uses depthwise separable convolutions.
A depthwise separable convolution decomposes a standard convolution into a depthwise convolution (one filter per input channel) followed by a $1 \times 1$ convolution.
The depthwise separable structure is more complex but has far fewer weights than a standard convolution.
The overall MobileNet architecture is not very deep.
MobileNet saves many parameters with a small drop in quality.
EfficientNet (Tan, Le, 2019) applies neural architecture search to find state-of-the-art networks.
The key insight of EfficientNet is compound scaling.
Simultaneously scaling network depth, width, and input resolution yields better performance than scaling a single dimension.
The neural architecture search in EfficientNet considers exponential scaling with exponents $\alpha$ (depth), $\beta$ (width) and $\gamma$ (resolution).
In EfficientNet, the total number of weights scales as the product of the scaling exponents $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$.
The efficiency landscape is often displayed on a plot with number of parameters on the x‑axis (fewer is better) and ImageNet top‑1 accuracy on the y‑axis (higher is better).
The Pareto frontier connects the best possible network for every size, and for every target quality the smallest possible network.
The EfficientNet family succeeded in defining this frontier.
EfficientNet remains the best underlying convolutional backbone.
EfficientNet is widely used in object detection and segmentation pipelines.
As weights of a layer change during training, the distribution of its outputs shifts.
The next layer must then continually re‑adapt.
Neurons that have reached saturation slow down retraining.
Internal covariate shift seriously impedes deep network training.

A layer that adds a bias $b$ to its input $u$, producing $x = u + b$, if normalised by subtracting the mean, $\hat{x} = x - \mathbb{E}[x]$, and then updating $b := b + \Delta b$, the normalised output does not change: $u + b + \Delta b - \mathbb{E}[u + b + \Delta b] = u + b - \mathbb{E}[u + b]$.
The biases grow without bound while the normalised output remains unchanged.
Training fails in this scenario.
Normalisation as a layer $\hat{x} = \text{Norm}(x, X)$ requires the entire dataset $X$ to compute gradients $\frac{\partial \text{Norm}}{\partial x}$ and $\frac{\partial \text{Norm}}{\partial X}$.
Normalisation as a layer requires computing the full covariance matrix $\text{Cov}[x] = \mathbb{E}_{x \in X}[xx^\top] - \mathbb{E}[x]\mathbb{E}[x]^\top$.
Computing the full covariance matrix is computationally prohibitive.
Batch normalisation normalises each feature component separately over the current mini‑batch.
For a component $x_k$, $\hat{x}_k = \frac{x_k - \mathbb{E}[x_k]}{\sqrt{\text{Var}[x_k]}}$.
The statistics $\mathbb{E}[x_k]$ and $\text{Var}[x_k]$ are computed on the current mini‑batch.
Normalising forces the activations into the linear regime of nonlinearities (e.g., the sigmoid).
Forcing activations into the linear regime can destroy the network’s capacity.
To remedy the destruction of capacity, learnable shift and scale parameters are introduced.
The learnable shift and scale parameters are: $y_k = \gamma_k \hat{x}_k + \beta_k = \gamma_k \frac{x_k - \mathbb{E}[x_k]}{\sqrt{\text{Var}[x_k]}} + \beta_k$.
$\gamma_k$ and $\beta_k$ are trained jointly with all other network weights.
Although originally motivated by reducing internal covariate shift, subsequent research showed that BN’s effectiveness does not really depend on this.
BN provides regularisation.
BN makes dropout often unnecessary.
BN significantly improves training.
One possible explanation for BN's effectiveness is that BN smooths the gradients, reducing the Lipschitz constant (Santurkar et al., 2019).
Another possible explanation is that BN decouples the learning of the direction and length of weight vectors, which improves training dynamics.
Yet another possible explanation is that BN helps achieve linear convergence in ordinary gradient descent.
Many normalisation methods share the same general operations: compute statistics over some set, normalise, then apply a learned scale and shift.
Normalisation methods differ in which dimensions the statistics are computed over.
The general form is: compute mean and variance over a specified set of axes, normalise, then transform with $\gamma$ and $\beta$.
Batch Normalization computes statistics over the mini‑batch dimension ($N$).
Batch Normalization is commonly used for images.
Batch Normalization averages the same feature over spatial dimensions and across the mini‑batch.
Layer Normalization computes statistics over all channels and spatial dimensions of a layer (all features of a single sample).
Layer Normalization does not average over the mini‑batch.
Layer Normalization is used mostly for vectors, in particular in transformers.
When using layer norm, the mini‑batch size is often one, so no mini‑batch statistics are available.
Layer norm normalises over the whole tensor of features for one sample.
Layer norm is essential for transformers, where large models rarely allow large mini‑batches.
Instance Normalization computes statistics over the spatial dimensions ($H$, $W$) only, separately per sample and per channel.
Instance Normalization is used, e.g., in AdaIN for style transfer.
Group Normalization splits channels into groups and normalises over each group together with the spatial dimensions.
Weight Standardization standardises the weights (per output channel) instead of normalising activations.
Weight Standardization effectively normalises the gradients during backpropagation.
Group norm combined with weight standardisation was used in BiT (Big Transfer).
Batch normalisation is not effective for recurrent networks (Laurent et al., 2016).
Recurrent batch normalisation was proposed (Cooijmans et al., 2016).
Weight normalisation (Salimans and Kingma, 2016) re‑parameterises the weight vector as $h_i = f\!\left(\frac{\gamma}{\|w_i\|} w_i^\top x + b_i\right)$.
Weight normalisation rescales the gradient, stabilises its norm, and brings the covariance matrix closer to the identity.
The landscape of normalisation methods remains an active research area (Huang et al., 2020).
Many problems involve sequential data: financial time series, sound, or text.
Unlike images, which are two‑dimensional structures naturally suited to CNNs, sequences are inherently one‑dimensional.
Sequence → single output: e.g., text classification – an entire news article is mapped to one category (sports, politics, science).
Single input → sequence: e.g., image captioning – a still image is converted into a variable‑length text description.
Sequence → sequence: e.g., machine translation – both input and output are sequences of variable length.
Sequence labelling: the output is a label for each input element, aligned with the input.

Examples of sequence labelling include part‑of‑speech tagging (a label for every word), video subtitle addition (each frame gets a text), and object tracking (segmenting an object consistently across video frames).
Applying a sliding window over the sequence cannot capture long‑range dependencies.
When reading a paragraph, one needs to remember what occurred many words earlier for the ending to make sense.
The crucial missing capability is the ability to retain information across arbitrary time spans.
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) maintain a hidden state updated as each element is processed.
The computational graph appears to contain cycles ($s_i = h(x_i, x_{i+1}, \dots, s_{i-1})$).
Backpropagation is performed by unrolling the recurrence in time: $y_6 = f(x_3, x_4, x_5, h(x_2, x_3, x_4, h(x_1, x_2, x_3, s_0)))$.
Practically, an RNN is a very deep network with many shared weights, causing notorious training difficulties.
A recurrent unit takes an input $x_t$ and the previous hidden state $h_{t-1}$ and outputs an updated hidden state $h_t$.
The same function with the exact same weights is applied at every time step.
Weight sharing enables the network to process sequences of arbitrary length.
A classical simple RNN cell is given by $h_t = g(A x_t + B h_{t-1})$.
In the formula, $A$ and $B$ are weight matrices and $g$ is a nonlinear activation such as $\tanh$ or ELU.
In slide notation, the RNN is written as $a_t = b + W s_{t-1} + U x_t$, $s_t = f(a_t)$, $o_t = c + V s_t$, $y_t = h(o_t)$.
In the slide notation, $f$ is the recurrent nonlinearity and $h$ the output function.
Weight sharing across time allows the same weights to handle variable‑length inputs.
Weight sharing is also a source of difficulty: the gradient of the loss with respect to a weight $w$ is a large sum because $w$ participates at every time step.
The influence of $w$ passes through repeated multiplication by the same weight matrix.
Because the state is repeatedly multiplied by $W$, the dynamics are governed by the spectral radius $\rho$ of $W$.
The spectral radius $\rho$ is roughly the factor by which multiplication scales vector length.
In the simplified case $h_t \approx W^t h_0$, we have $\|h_t\| \approx \rho^t \|h_0\|$.
If $\rho > 1$, activations and gradients explode exponentially with sequence length.
If $\rho > 1$, the explosion causes numerical overflow.
If $\rho < 1$, gradients vanish as they travel backwards.
Vanishing gradients destroy the influence of early sequence elements and prevent learning of long‑term dependencies.
Exploding gradients are handled by gradient clipping.
In gradient clipping, if the gradient norm exceeds a threshold, the gradient vector is rescaled so that its norm equals the threshold.
Gradient clipping can be thought of as keeping the update from flying off a steep “wall” in the loss landscape and gently redirecting it back to the normal regime.
Pascanu et al. (2013) studied this behaviour and showed that RNNs have bifurcation points where such instabilities originate.
Clipping is theoretically and practically sound: it does not distort the direction of the gradient catastrophically.
The vanishing gradient problem is far more challenging.
The vanishing gradient problem is addressed by architectures such as LSTM and GRU.
For sequence labelling tasks, it is unnatural to look only at past context.
A bidirectional RNN runs two separate recurrent networks: one left‑to‑right, one right‑to‑left.
At position $t$, the left‑to‑right hidden state captures left context and the right‑to‑left hidden state captures right context.
The outputs of the two hidden states are merged via a classification head.
For the left-to-right RNN: $s_t = \sigma(b + W s_{t-1} + U x_t)$.
For the right-to-left RNN: $s'_t = \sigma(b' + W' s'_{t+1} + U' x_t)$.
The output is given by $o_t = c + V s_t + V' s'_t$, $y_t = h(o_t)$.
Bidirectional RNNs are standard unless the problem prohibits using future context.
Examples of problems prohibiting future context: language modelling requires predicting the next word using only left context; real‑time tracking can look only a few frames ahead.
The principle of bidirectional processing generalises to any recurrent architecture.
Vanishing gradients occur because the gradient must repeatedly pass through multiplication by $W$.
To preserve long‑term memory, a shortcut for gradients is needed, analogous to skip connections in ResNet.
The shortcut for gradients is called the constant error carousel.
LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1995/1997; modern form by Gers & Schmidhuber, 2000) constructs a complex unit that explicitly controls memory.
The LSTM cell maintains a cell state $c_t$ and a hidden state $h_t$.
Gates control information flow in the LSTM cell.
Candidate cell state: $c'_t = \tanh(W_{xc} x_t + W_{hc} h_{t-1} + b_{c'})$.
Input gate: $i_t = \sigma(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + b_i)$.
Forget gate: $f_t = \sigma(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + b_f)$.
Output gate: $o_t = \sigma(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + b_o)$.
Cell state update: $c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot c'_t$.
Hidden state: $h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t)$.
If $f_t = 1$, then $c_t = c_{t-1} + i_t \odot c'_t$.
When $f_t = 1$, $\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}} = 1$, creating the constant error carousel.
Peephole connections address the case where the output gate closes and LSTM behaviour becomes independent of the cell state.
Peephole connections add the cell state directly to the gate computations.
$i_t = \sigma(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + W_{pi} c_{t-1} + b_i)$.
$f_t = \sigma(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + W_{pf} c_{t-1} + b_f)$.
$o_t = \sigma(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + W_{po} c_{t-1} + b_o)$.
Numerous LSTM variations exist.
“LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey” (Greff et al., 2015) showed that some significantly simpler architectures (with one gate fewer) perform nearly as well.
GRU (Cho et al., 2014) also implements the constant error carousel but with a simpler design.
GRU merges the cell state and hidden state into a single state $h_t$.
GRU uses only two gates.
Update gate: $u_t = \sigma(W_{xu} x_t + W_{hu} h_{t-1} + b_u)$.
Reset gate: $r_t = \sigma(W_{xr} x_t + W_{hr} h_{t-1} + b_r)$.
Candidate hidden state: $h'_t = \tanh(W_{xh'} x_t + W_{hh'} (r_t \odot h_{t-1}))$.
Hidden state update: $h_t = (1 - u_t) \odot h'_t + u_t \odot h_{t-1}$.
GRU uses 6 weight matrices (vs. 8 or 11 with peepholes in LSTM).
GRU has fewer parameters than LSTM.
GRU is only slightly worse than LSTM.
Under a fixed computational budget, one can fit more GRU units, making it competitive or even preferable.
Other variations of RNN architectures exist.
Józefowicz, Zaremba, and Sutskever (2015) performed a large evolutionary search over RNN architectures.
Józefowicz, Zaremba, and Sutskever (2015) identified several interesting alternative structures.
